title: Solar water disinfection (SODIS) in clear plastic bottles
summary: Fill clear plastic bottles with clear water and lay them in full sun for at least 6 hours. Sunlight and warmth cut most diarrhoea bacteria and Giardia; Cryptosporidium and most viruses drop far only in ideal conditions. In a Canadian winter the sun is too weak: boil or chlorinate instead. It costs nothing, but it does not remove chemicals, salt or mud, and it needs sun.

materials.item: Clear PET plastic bottles, 2 litres or smaller, unscratched, labels removed
Corrugated metal sheet or a sunny roof to lay bottles on

steps.text: Pick bottles: clear (not coloured) PET plastic, marked with recycling code 1, 2 litres or smaller, not badly scratched. Peel the labels off (Eawag manual, SSWM SODIS).
steps.warn: Never use bottles that held fuel, pesticide or other chemicals. Washing doesn't make them safe.

steps.text: Check the water is clear. Fill a bottle, stand it on a printed page or a sign with letters about 1.5 cm high, and look down through the water. If you can't read the letters, the water is too cloudy; readable means under about 30 NTU, clear enough for SODIS (SSWM SODIS).
Clear cloudy water first: let it settle in a bucket for a few hours and pour off the top, or pour it through a folded clean cloth.
Fill the bottle to the top and cap it. Eawag, who wrote the method, no longer recommends shaking it part-full first (Eawag manual).

Lay the bottles flat in full sun, on a metal roof, a sheet of corrugated metal or anything reflective or dark, from morning. Reflective sheets and dark backgrounds help a little (by under 30 %), not enough to cut the exposure time (Eawag manual, SSWM SODIS). Don't let them fall into shade.

Leave them at least 6 hours in sun or light cloud. If more than half the sky is cloudy, leave them 2 full days. In continuous rain SODIS does not work: collect rainwater instead (SSWM SODIS, CDC Yellow Book).
Drink straight from the bottle or pour into a clean cup. Use the water within a day.
Replace bottles when the surface gets badly scratched or cloudy: it turns opaque, typically after a few months of use (Eawag manual, SSWM SODIS).

notes:
## How it works

UV-A light in sunlight damages germs, and warming the water speeds that up. Together they inactivate bacteria and some parasites (SSWM SODIS). Of the intestinal bacteria in one Eawag study, Salmonella Typhimurium was the hardest to inactivate and cholera the easiest (Eawag SODIS). Eawag's manual says the drop is large for bacteria and Giardia, but only in favourable conditions, such as warm water and a high sun dose, for Cryptosporidium, amoebae and most viruses: in one PET-bottle study a rotavirus needed over 30 hours of sun for a 1,000-fold drop (Eawag manual). So the full exposure time matters. Oxygen in the water takes part in the reaction (SSWM SODIS), but Eawag's manual says the water picks up enough as you fill the bottle, so the shake in the steps is optional (Eawag manual).

Heat helps: above about 45 °C, heat and UV-A work together and less time is needed (SSWM SODIS), and Eawag says it works best at 50 °C or more (Eawag SODIS). Without a thermometer, give it the full time.

## What SODIS does not do

- It does not remove chemical pollution such as arsenic, fluoride or farm chemicals (SSWM SODIS, Eawag manual). Fuel, heavy metals, salt and poisons stay in the water too.
- It does not clear mud or cloudiness: you must do that first.
- It does not protect water once it's poured into a dirty container.
- It needs strong, steady sun. SSWM calls it strongly weather-dependent and best between latitudes 15° and 35° (SSWM SODIS), and Eawag's manual says its 6-hour guidance does not apply beyond 30° latitude, where the sun can be much weaker, especially in winter (Eawag manual). All of Canada lies farther north, so in winter, with a low sun and short days, don't count on it: boil or use chlorine.

## Other ways to make water safe

| Method | What it does | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Boiling | Kills germs | Most reliable. Bring to a rolling boil for 1 minute (at least 2 minutes above 2,000 m, Health Canada BWA). Needs fuel |
| Chlorine | Kills most germs | See chlorine. Use the right dose and wait 30 minutes |
| Filtering | Removes germs (fine filters) and some chemicals (carbon) | See [Two-bucket gravity water filter](#guides/build_gravity_water_filter) |
| SODIS | Cuts bacteria and Giardia; weak on Cryptosporidium and most viruses | Free, needs strong sun, clear water, bottles and time |

Combine methods when the source is poor: settle, filter through cloth, then SODIS or boil.

## Bottles

PET is the clear, light, slightly flexible plastic of most drink bottles. Use clear PET bottles of 2 litres or smaller, no more than 10 cm deep lying down (Eawag manual, SSWM SODIS). SSWM accepts glass bottles too, but window glass blocks almost all the UV and PVC bottles aren't recommended (SSWM SODIS), and Eawag says polycarbonate (recycling symbol 7) must not be used because it can release BPA (Eawag manual), so PET is the simple choice. Eawag found only traces of plasticisers leaching from PET bottles in the sun, well below WHO drinking-water guideline values (Eawag manual).
